summary:
The Cook Islands is a self-governing state in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to the Cook Islands, while local criminal law governs conduct within the territory.

Male same-sex conduct was criminalised under sections 154 and 155 of the 1969 Crimes Act, a colonial-era statute carrying up to seven years for sex between men and five years for "any indecent act with or upon any other male", with consent explicitly not a defence. Parliament voted on 14 April 2023 to remove those provisions through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. Reporting at the time described the provisions as never enforced, and enforcement in living memory was essentially absent, so the repeal removed a held-over statutory risk rather than an active prosecution threat.

Decriminalisation took a decade of contested legislative passage. A draft Crimes Bill drafted with New Zealand assistance in 2017 would have struck sections 154 and 155, and a select committee that year recommended removal, but MPs later backtracked; in October 2020 parliament deferred the Crimes Bill report by a further three months, continuing a pattern of kick-down-the-road handling before the 2023 vote. A note attached to the successful bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the same legislation adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000, so marriage and partner recognition are not available locally.

Advocacy came from the Te Tiare Association, the country's only LGBTI community group, whose members publicly challenged the law's homophobic framing; parliament opened public submissions on the Crimes Bill in August 2017, with the association's submission before the select committee and lawyers expected to address penalties and sentencing. Reporting in 2020 described the Cook Islands as historically accepting of same-sex relationships, with the anti-LGBT taboo introduced through colonisation into a society of roughly 21,000 people.
tangentialFactors:
The legislative history shows a persistent gap between committee-level intent and final passage: recommendations to remove the 1969 sections were made in 2017, reversed, and deferred again in 2020, so statutory reform in this jurisdiction has historically required sustained external and local pressure rather than following a fixed timetable.

The Crimes Amendment Bill couples decriminalisation with substantive additions on sexual abuse and assault, indicating that the Parliament's framing of the reform was broader than consensual conduct alone.

With a population of about 21,000 and a single national LGBTI organisation, the scale of civic infrastructure is small; legal change has been driven substantially by one community group working alongside New Zealand-assisted drafters.

Pre-contact social history is cited in reporting as distinct from the imported colonial taboo, which bears on how hostility to LGBT people is localised rather than uniform across the population.
localsOnly:
Residents gained statutory relief from the 1969 Crimes Act provisions on 1 June 2023, and the same package of amendments strengthens protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault under domestic law.

Marriage for same-sex couples remains unavailable under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000, affecting resident couples' access to marital status, inheritance and next-of-kin recognition locally.

The Te Tiare Association has operated as the representative body for the LGBTI community in submissions to Parliament's select committee and in public advocacy for repeal.

Residents hold New Zealand nationality and travel on New Zealand passports, so citizenship, consular protection and travel documentation are governed from Wellington rather than by local statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity documents or gender markers for trans people in the Cook Islands, either for local documents or for New Zealand-issued passports used by residents; that position is unresolved here.

Whether the repeal produced any change in practice for trans-specific conduct, or whether other provisions of the Crimes Act continue to reach gender-nonconforming behaviour, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Hate-crime provisions, anti-discrimination protections and any enforcement guidance covering gender identity rather than sexual orientation are not covered by these sources.

The outcome of the August 2017 submission process and the specific penalties discussed by the lawyers who appeared before the select committee are not recorded in the inventory.

Facilities, healthcare access and any screening at the border that could disclose a traveller's gender history are unsourced for this jurisdiction.
